newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU in disarray over plant relocation moves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU in disarray over plant relocation moves.

text.p: What is it that attracts firms to Ireland's Galway and Germany's Saxony away from regions in the centre of the European Union with high purchasing power?

The answer, which is increasingly bothering the countries which lose out and vexing the European Commission, is favourable tax regimes, high subsidies and usually a cheaper and more flexible labour force.
In theory this should not have happened in the EU's border-free market created in 1993, at least regarding tax and social rules.

But the 15-nation bloc has so far proved incapable of agreeing on a common corporate tax, along with many other taxes, and when it comes to social rules most countries, notably Britain, still prefer to go it alone.

While nothing can be done to stop Britain, Spain, Portugal and the former east Germany from offering better labour conditions, the Commission is looking at ways to prevent tax competition and discourage national governments from luring foreign companies with generous cash grants.

"Neither present competition rules, nor the structural fund regulations, can sufficiently prevent companies from abusing the system by moving their activities in such a way as to maximise the aid they receive from public sources," European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies, who is in charge of EU structural funds, said last week.
Warning that this could "no longer be tolerated", Wulf-Mathies said she had the "firm intention" to prevent such behaviour in the near future.

Although she did not mention any names, Wulf-Mathies was reacting to Renault's decision to close a plant in Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs, and increase production in the Spanish northern province of Castille-Leon. The province is eligible for EU and Spanish funds as one of the EU's poorest.

EU and industry officials have also pointed the finger at the decision by Boston Scientific Corp, a high-growth U.S. medical equipment specialist, to close its operations in Denmark and Belgium and expand in Galway, western Ireland.
"They closed down in Belgium and went to Ireland because Ireland is more subsidised," Baudouin Velge, chairman of the Federation of Belgian Enterprises, told Reuters.
STRUCTURAL FUNDS AND DIFFERING TAX REGIMES

EU structural funds, worth some 35 billion European currency units (ECUs) ($40.1 billion) a year, are a mix of grants to help the bloc's poorer regions to help catch up with their healthier neighbours.
The need for this is rarely contested even by the EU's rich manufacturing countries as properous regions are more likely to become good consumers.

Different tax regimes are the other tricky problem. Ireland currently offers European manufacturers the best tax environment. The rate of corporation tax there is 36 percent -- which is about the EU's average -- but it applies a reduced 10 percent tax for manufacturing firms.
But according to Boston Scientific's chief financial officer Larry Best Ireland's secret weapon for atracting businesses is more than just financial support and lower taxes.

"They went out of the way in attracting partnerships: we committed to build and to grow and they committed to help us," Best told Reuters on the telephone from the company's headquarters in Natik, Massachussets.
He compared Ireland's "good employee base" to Belgium's: "Just ask anybody about dealing with the unions in Belgium" he said.
Belgian authorities and the workforce "view the corporate community as the enemy."
REPERCUSSIONS OF RENAULT'S DECISION

Tens of thousands of angry Belgian and other European workers took to the streets of Brussels last Sunday in an unprecedented march for jobs calling on governments to prevent other Renault-like moves.
EU social affairs ministers who met in Rotterdam last weekend said there should be a clear code of conduct for multinationals both opening and closing factories.

The French carmaker maintains that its decision to close the Belgian plant north of Brussels is part of a global restructuring drive to survive huge losses in 1996 and respond to overcapacity in Europe.

Other companies, such as Britain's Hoover, have in the past relocated their European operations, but none has attracted such a public outcry. This has led French Industry Minister Frank Borotra to accuse EU officials of double-standards.

"When Victor Co of Japan Ltd relocated out of Lorraine, when Hoover pulled out of Bourgogne, when Grundig AG closed down its Creutzvald activities, I don't recall getting support from the European Commission," Borotra said recently.
And yet there is little the Commission can do.

A study expected by its competition services shortly is only to look at subsidy hopping -- a situation which does not apply to Renault since it got no support either from the EU or the Belgian authorities for its Vilvoorde plant. The same goes for Boston Scientific.
Wulf-Mathies's plan to reform the way the EU's structural funds are spent may have some more bite but is not expected to materialise before the next century.

Future policy changes could subject EU support to investments to the long-term creation of jobs and non-destruction of employment elsewhere in the bloc, Commission sources said. The reform is part of the overall review of the Union's budget after 1999. ($ = 0.873 European Currency Unit ECUs)
